content.title: About
content.content: Ground beef is minced meat obtained from various cuts of a beef carcass. It has a rich, meaty flavor, a soft texture, and is used in a wide range of dishes, from burgers and meatballs to sauces and fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ground beef is often made from less expensive cuts such as chuck, shoulder, or brisket, making it an economical protein source.
Different countries have signature ground‑beef dishes: Russian kotleti, Italian Bolognese, Mexican tacos.
Ground beef is sold with varying fat percentages, from lean (5‑10 % fat) to regular (15‑20 % fat).
When stored properly, fresh ground beef lasts 1‑2 days in the fridge and 3‑4 months in the freezer.
The term “first‑grade ground beef” indicates meat without added bones or connective tissue.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Ground beef provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc in beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Ground beef contains creatine, which may help improve muscular strength.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Raw meat can harbor pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Higher‑fat blends increase calorie density and may raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Pre‑seasoned ground beef may contain preservatives like nitrites, which should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use ground beef for burgers, meatballs, sauces, stuffed peppers, pies, and many other recipes. Before cooking, trim excess fat if desired and season to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ground beef refrigerated at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for 3‑4 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Bologna is a cooked sausage made from beef, pork, and sometimes turkey, seasoned with spices and flavorings. It has a delicate pink color, soft texture, and a mildly sweet taste. The product is often sliced thinly and used in sandwiches, salads, and appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bologna first appeared in the United States in the late 19th century and is named after the Italian city of Bologna, although the recipe differs from traditional Italian mortadella.
Traditionally it contains a blend of beef and pork in a 70/30 ratio, but modern versions may include turkey or chicken.
The sausage is lightly smoked, giving it a characteristic aroma without a strong smoky flavor.
Bologna is frequently used in the classic Cuban sandwich and in “corned‑beef” style dishes.
In the U.S., bologna is one of the most popular ready‑to‑eat cold cuts for quick snacks.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Bologna provides about 12–14 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron in the sausage helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bologna is rich in B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The sausage contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Bologna often contains 800–1200 mg of sodium per 100 g, which can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Nitrites are added to extend shelf life, and excessive intake may pose health concerns.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the meat components.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Bologna contains saturated fats, so people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bologna is typically sliced thin and used in sandwiches, salads, charcuterie boards, or as an ingredient in hot dishes such as pasta. It can be briefly warmed in a skillet or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bologna in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, it is best consumed within 5–7 days. When frozen, it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Cantaloupe nectar is a sweet, refreshing drink made from ripe cantaloupe flesh, water and a small amount of sugar. It has a bright orange colour, the aroma of fresh cantaloupe and a light fruity sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cantaloupe (Cucumis melo) belongs to the gourd family and is cultivated in warm regions worldwide.
Nectar retains most of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh cantaloupe, but in a more concentrated form.
In many countries the drink is traditionally served during the summer season as a refreshing beverage.
The beta‑carotene content gives the nectar its vivid orange hue and makes it a source of provitamin A.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted in the body to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C helps protect cells from oxidative stress and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie beverage
items.content: Cantaloupe nectar is low in calories, making it a light refreshing option.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s hydration levels.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some versions contain added sugar, which should be considered by people with diabetes or those monitoring sugar intake.

items.title: Allergy to gourds
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to foods from the gourd family.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial products may contain preservatives; choose additive‑free options if this is a concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled; it can be added to cocktails, smoothies, punches, or used as a base for fruit desserts. It pairs well with mint, lime and berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: After opening, keep the nectar refrigerated in a tightly sealed container for up to 5‑7 days. Unopened product should be stored in a cool, dry place at temperatures up to 25 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Ramen bowl is a ready‑to‑eat set of ramen noodles in a vegetable broth, topped with fresh vegetables and a boiled egg. The dish is vegetarian as it contains no meat, but includes an egg for protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional ramen originates from Japan, but vegetarian versions have become popular worldwide.
The egg in ramen is often served soft‑boiled so the yolk gently runs into the broth, adding a creamy texture.
Vegetable ramen commonly includes seaweed, soy sprouts, and spinach, boosting vitamin and mineral content.
Quick preparation (5‑7 minutes) makes ramen a favorite among students and busy professionals.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The egg provides about 6 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vegetables and noodles contain B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Green vegetables such as spinach and broccoli are high in vitamin C and carotenoids, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain noodles supply fiber, promoting digestive health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The dish contains minimal saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs should avoid this ramen as it can trigger reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared broth often contains high levels of salt; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some broths are flavored with MSG, which may cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the broth, add the noodles, vegetables, and boiled egg. Stir, let sit for 1‑2 minutes, then enjoy. Optional toppings include soy sauce, chili oil, or toasted sesame seeds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry ingredients (noodles, seasonings) in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked broth and vegetables should be refrigerated and used within 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Gluten-Free Waffles are crisp treats made from a blend of gluten‑free flours (such as rice, buckwheat or corn), eggs, milk and a touch of sugar. They are suitable for people with celiac disease or anyone following a gluten‑free diet while preserving the classic taste and texture of traditional waffles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free waffles often use a mix of rice and corn flour, giving them a light golden crust.
They can be made sweet or savory – herbs, cheese, or spices are added to the batter for a savory twist.
Traditional Belgian waffles have deeper pockets, which hold more syrup or berries.
Gluten‑free versions frequently contain more protein thanks to added eggs or dairy.
Waffles reheat well in a toaster or oven, staying crunchy.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and dairy in the batter provide a good source of complete protein, essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Gluten‑free flours and eggs contain thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Buckwheat and corn flours used in many recipes add a modest amount of iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Absence of gluten makes these waffles safe for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and complex carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Gluten‑free waffles often contain eggs and milk, which can trigger reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Like any waffle, they can be calorie‑rich, especially when butter, sugar, or toppings are added.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Some ready‑made gluten‑free mixes include added sugar; people monitoring blood glucose should check the label.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt is commonly added for flavor; choose low‑sodium options if you have high blood pressure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gluten‑free waffles with fresh berries, fruit puree, honey, nut butter, or low‑fat yogurt. They also work as a base for savory sandwiches with ham, cheese, and vegetables. For a healthier option, choose toppings without added sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked waffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in a toaster or oven until crisp before serving.
